bio.en: Jiaona Zhang (JZ) is Senior Vice President of Product at Webflow, a lecturer at Stanford teaching product management, and a longtime product leader at Airbnb, Dropbox, and WeWork.
bio.zh: Jiaona Zhang（JZ）是 Webflow 的产品高级副总裁、斯坦福产品管理课程讲师，也是在 Airbnb、Dropbox、WeWork 任职多年的产品负责人。

summary.en: JZ digs into the most common mistakes early PMs make, the concept of 'minimal lovable products' versus MVPs, and her unique frameworks for roadmapping, prioritization, and OKRs. She shares how to structure your first 90 days as a product leader, lessons from her wild year at WeWork, the best product and leadership advice she's received, and the story of Airbnb Plus and where it went wrong. A recurring theme: become known for being excellent at something specific, because reputation attracts responsibility.
summary.zh: JZ 深入剖析了初级 PM 最常见的错误、“最小化可爱产品”（minimal lovable products）与 MVP 的区别，以及她独特的路线图、优先级排序与 OKR 框架。她分享了作为产品领导者如何规划新公司的前 90 天、在 WeWork 疯狂一年的教训、她收到过最好的产品与领导力建议，以及 Airbnb Plus 的故事与失败原因。一个反复出现的主题是：让自己以“在某件具体的事上极其出色”而闻名，因为声誉会吸引责任。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think it's really important to become really good at and also known for something. You could be known for shepherding like the most complex launches because you're just so good at quarterbacking. Working with go-to--market teams and cross-functional stakeholders that could be like your thing. You could be known for working on the most technically complex problems, find something that you can be really, really good at. And the reason I give that advice is because when you do that, you can crush the projects that you get because you're making a name for yourself, reputation, and then you are giving more responsibility. People tend to flock and give responsibility to the people that are known for being excellent at something.
turns.zh: 我认为真正精通某项技能并因此闻名至关重要。你或许因能出色地统筹最复杂的项目而声名远扬，或许因与市场团队和跨职能利益相关者密切合作而成为行家，或许因专攻技术难题而备受推崇。我给出这条建议的核心在于，当你专注于某项擅长之事时，你就能在接手的项目中大显身手——因为你已树立了专业声誉，获得了更多信任与授权。人们往往会主动追随并赋予那些在某方面卓有建树的人更多责任。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Thanks for having me. I'm so excited to be here.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请我。我很兴奋能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's 100% my pleasure. Amongst your many accomplishments, you teach product management at Stanford, which sounds very fancy. How long have you been doing this at this point?
turns.zh: 这完全是我的荣幸。在您众多的成就中，您在斯坦福大学教授产品管理课程，这听起来相当了不起。您从事这项工作多久了？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think six years. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我想是六年了。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So my question, the real question I want to ask about this is, in that time you've seen a lot of new PMs and you've seen these PMs succeed, you've seen some fail. What are the most common mistakes that you find new PMs make in this experience of helping new PMs get into the field?
turns.zh: 好的。那么我的问题，我真正想问的是，在这段时间里，您见过许多新入行的产品经理，也见过他们成功或失败的案例。在帮助新产品经理入行这个过程中，您发现他们最常犯的错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think something that is really hard to untrain, but I think every human does it, is you jump to solutions. And so one of the biggest things I see, not just in my course but also just as a PM and some of the mistakes that you make as a PM is the idea of you get really attached to a solution, a way of implementing something that you can see in your head that you want to build. (00:05:16): And so that's the first thing I really want to unteach in our course. And so a lot of people will literally come in, they'll be like, "I want to build X startup" or "I want to do this thing," or "I'm in blank school and I've been doing a lot of research on this particular area." And so untraining that and being like, "Hey, we're going to go out there. We are not going to think at all about the thing that you want to build, but instead we're going to be focused on users and people in the real world and their problems. And the first step is to understand their problems and then understand if there's an opportunity here as opposed to, 'Hey, you want to build X thing for Y person.'" So that's the biggest mistake that you really have to unteach and retrain thinking around.
turns.zh: 我认为有些错误很难改掉，但每个人都会犯，就是急于找到解决方案。就我而言，无论是在课程中还是作为产品经理，您会发现最常见的错误是，人们过于执着于某个解决方案，执着于自己脑海中构想的某种实施方式。（00:05:16）所以这是我们课程中最想纠正的思维模式。很多学员一来就会说：“我想创办X初创公司”或者“我想做这个项目”，或者“我在某某学校，针对某个特定领域做了大量研究”。所以我们要纠正这种思维，告诉他们：“我们要走出去，完全不去想你想建造的东西，而是要关注用户和现实世界中的人们以及他们的问题。第一步是理解他们的需求，然后判断这里是否有机会，而不是想‘嘿，我想为Y群体打造X产品’。” 所以这是最需要纠正和重新培养思维模式的错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Does a lot of this come from people want to get into product management because they think "Finally I'll have the power, finally I'll be able to tell people what to build, finally my ideas really going to matter?" Is that where a lot lobby comes from?
turns.zh: 很多新人进入产品管理领域，是因为他们认为“终于能掌控大局了，终于能告诉别人该做什么了，终于能让自己的想法真正发挥作用了”吗？这是否是很多人的误区？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think there's a part of that. One of the first things I teach is you're not a CEO, you're, you're not here... You actually have very little true authority because you don't actually manage anyone. A lot of it is all through influence, and so that is also a piece where you have to kind of untrain that thinking. I do think a lot of people come into the product role thinking that I get to call the shots, I get to make the decisions, I get to decide what gets built. And really your job is not that. Your job is to understand here are the opportunities, and then you're kind of pulling together all the different possibilities and you're really editing. So I do think it comes from desire for a lot of people thinking that's what the product role is when it actually isn't.
turns.zh: 我认为这部分原因确实存在。我首先教给学员的是，你不是CEO，你没有管理权限。你实际上管理不了任何人。很多权力都来自于影响力，所以这也是需要纠正的思维模式。我确实发现很多新人进入产品角色时，以为自己能呼风唤雨、拍板定案，但实际上并非如此。你的职责是理解机会所在，然后整合各种可能性并进行筛选。所以我认为这种误区源于很多人的期待与现实不符。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's go to the other side of this question. We talked about what mistakes new PMs make. I'm curious, what's the biggest product mistake that you've made?
turns.zh: 那么让我们来谈谈另一个问题方向。我们讨论了新产品经理常犯的错误。我很好奇，您自己犯过的最大产品管理错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Wow, that's a good one. It's so interesting. I feel like as product people, we're always making mistakes and we're always learning. Maybe I'll give an example from Airbnb since you and I were both there. And this one does stand out to me, we were working on this concept called Airbnb Plus. If you took a step back, what we were really trying to do is to be like, "Hey, not everyone trusts Airbnb in terms of... It's a platform. It's not like it's managed inventory, it's not a hotel. How do you go in and really make sure that all the Airbnbs are meeting the quality bar?" But I do think we were very solution-first, and I think we're also competitor afraid at the time. So it was during a time where there were managed marketplaces, there were the Sonders out there, and I think that as a company we're very much like "[inaudible 00:07:36] what are we going to do in the world of managed marketplaces?" (00:07:38): And so we went really hard down the solution space. We essentially were like, "Let's go inspect our inventory, let's actually try to manage our inventory more." And really what we should have done is taken a step back and be like, "What's the real problem? The real problem is people want to know what they're getting themselves into. We need to represent the homes a lot better." And I think the other piece here that's really important is, what, as a company is your strategic strength and what's in your wheelhouse? So for example, Airbnb, we weren't that strong in operations. Again, we're this platform with this marketplace. And so if you don't have that muscle and then you're asking the company, the teams to essentially build it from the ground up, that's really, really difficult. Not to mention the unit economics, are the unit economics actually going to work even as you scale?
turns.zh: 哇，这真是个好例子。太有意思了。作为产品人，我们总是在不断犯错、不断学习。或许我可以举个Airbnb的例子，毕竟你和我都曾在那里工作过。Airbnb Plus这个项目让我印象深刻。回过头来看，我们当时真正想解决的问题是：“嘿，不是每个人都信任Airbnb这个平台的。它毕竟不是酒店，也不是集中管理的库存平台。如何确保所有Airbnb房源都能达到质量标准？”但当时我们过于以解决方案为导向，还深受竞争对手的困扰。当时有许多集中管理的市场平台，比如Sonders，我们公司当时就在思考：“在集中管理的市场领域，我们该如何突围？”（00:07:38）于是我们一头扎进解决方案的开发中，本质上是想：“让我们去检查我们的库存，真正尝试管理我们的库存。”但我们真正应该做的是退一步，问问自己：“真正的问题是什么？问题在于人们想知道自己将面临怎样的体验。我们需要更好地展示房源信息。” 另一个关键点是，作为一家公司，什么是我们的战略优势和专长领域？比如Airbnb，我们在运营方面并不强大。毕竟我们只是一个平台型的市场平台。如果没有这方面的能力，却要求团队从零开始打造，那实在太难了。更不用说单位经济效益问题——即便规模扩大了，经济效益真的能行得通吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I feel like Airbnb Plus is an untold story that somebody should tell and that could be its own podcast, I guess.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得Airbnb Plus是个未被讲述的故事，应该有人把它做成播客。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: You and I can tell it.
turns.zh: 你和我可以来讲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We could tell this could be Airbnb Plus The Hidden Story. As you said, the problem it was trying to solve was people don't really trust... They don't want to even consider Airbnb because it's like, "No, I don't want to stay in someone's home. I don't know what it'll be. It's unpredictable." And so as an outsider, it felt like a really clever approach. "We're going to vet them, we're going to make sure they're awesome. There's a minimum bar." And I guess this is the question is do you think it was just like "This is never possible because we'll never make money as a business doing this because we don't make that much per booking and investing time, resources, sending people pillows, all that stuff is ever going to be economical"? Or do you think there was a path that was just not executed well?
turns.zh: 我们可以把它命名为《Airbnb Plus：不为人知的故事》。正如你所说，Airbnb Plus试图解决的问题是人们不信任……他们甚至不愿考虑Airbnb，因为他们觉得：“不，我不想住在别人家里。我不知道会是什么样子。太不可预测了。” 作为局外人，我觉得这是一个很巧妙的解决方案。“我们会去审核房源，确保它们都很棒。设定一个最低标准。” 问题在于，你们觉得这是不可能的吗？因为作为商业行为，这样做根本赚不到钱——毕竟每次预订的利润不高，而投入时间、资源、给房东送枕头之类的成本又太高了？还是说你们认为当时的路径只是执行不力？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think there wasn't really a clear path. I think there was less of-
turns.zh: 我觉得当时并没有明确的路径。更多的是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's my impression.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也这么觉得。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Exactly. And it was more just like if you understood... Again, this is what my point around unit economics, there are things where I think you have magical thinking around unit economics. You're like, "When we get to the scale of X, it's all going to work out. We can make these things happen." I think you actually need to really make sure that unit economics work quite at the beginning. That is definitely one lesson. And I think the other thing is, and going back to spirit of what are you trying to achieve. If you're trying to achieve this idea of really knowing the quality of the place, and for a platform like Airbnb, the right way to go about doing is through our reviews, through our guest reviews, which are essentially free as opposed to literally sending out inspectors. (00:09:51): And I think that the other things are if you can get signal on what are the things around quality that people care about, is it cleaning? Is it, "Hey, I'm locked out"? And I think that there are other solutions besides inspection that then get at that. So for example, it is actually cheaper to go send everyone a lockbox than to deploy an inspector and go look at your property. It is actually cheaper to maybe do a partnership with a bunch of cleaners in different local areas and then get that as part of the fee, as opposed to doing the inspection. So again, it's really about what are you really trying to achieve? What is the user problem in each of these areas and can you target that problem with the particular listing that you're looking at? (00:10:33): And so I personally don't believe the unit economics ever would've really worked out. I think we should have known that or we should have dug into that more at the very beginning and then to get very tailored instead of one blunt instrument to solve it all, "Hey, we're going to go inspect." It's like what is the problem for this listing and what's the best solution to fix that problem?
turns.zh: 没错。再说一次，这就是我关于单位经济学的观点。有些情况下，我觉得人们对单位经济学存在魔法思维。比如你会想：“等我们规模达到X，就一切顺利了。我们就能把事情搞定了。” 但实际上，你必须从一开始就确保单位经济学能真正奏效。这绝对是一个教训。另外，我认为关键还在于你要回归到初衷——你到底想达成什么目标？如果你想真正了解房源质量，那么对于像Airbnb这样的平台来说，正确的做法应该是通过用户评价来实现，而非派遣检查员实地检查。（00:09:51）还有，如果你能准确把握用户关心的质量要素，比如清洁问题、被锁在门外等情况，那就更容易找到解决方案了。比如，为所有房源配备智能锁箱的成本，要比派遣检查员实地检查低得多。与其派检查员，不如与当地多家清洁公司合作，将清洁服务纳入房源费用，这样更划算。所以关键在于，你到底想解决什么问题？每个领域的用户痛点是什么？你能否针对具体房源量身定制解决方案？（00:10:33）所以我个人认为单位经济学模式本就注定失败。我们本该在一开始就预见到问题，深入研究现有方案，而不是一味追求简单粗暴的解决方案，比如派检查员上门检查。关键在于：针对具体房源，问题出在哪里？最优解是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple things that I think are important product leadership lessons here. One is Airbnb and Brian and many great leaders are famous for imagining the ideal situation, imagining the great end result and then working backwards. And often that leads to great results when you're being really ambitious and "I don't know how we're going to get there, we're just going to shoot big and hopefully we figure it out." Sometimes it works out. In this case it didn't work out. And what you're finding, maybe you even knew this early on, is just like there's no possible world where this could have worked in this approach. Is there anything you've learned about just when to think big and not even like "Forget it. We're going to figure it out. I know this seems impossible, but we're just going to try it anyway"? Do you have any kind of framework of when to think big, then just go for it? Versus, "Oh, let's just work out the math today," is this ever possible?
turns.zh: 这里有几个我认为很重要的产品领导力教训。首先，Airbnb、布莱恩以及许多优秀的领导者都以想象理想状态、构想最终目标并从此倒推而闻名。当你雄心勃勃时，这种方法往往能带来出色成果：“我不知道怎么实现目标，但我们要大胆尝试，希望能找到解决方案。”有时确实能成功，但这次却失败了。而你发现的，或许你早就有过类似认识，那就是这种方法在任何情况下都不可能成功。对于“大胆尝试，事后再理清头绪”这种思路，你有什么经验吗？有没有什么框架能指导何时该大胆尝试，何时该按部就班？比如“哦，今天先把数学问题解决了”，这种方法可行吗？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think it's really important for every company to be dreaming big. If you don't have a big vision, it's really hard for you to innovate, but you got to couple that really big vision with thoughtfulness around your execution. And so I think that one of the biggest tips I have is how do to be clear about the phase that you're in? So I think it's totally fine to be like, "Hey, we are going to try X for six months, three months, whatever it is, and we're explicitly going to go learn these types of things. We're going to learn why are people? Are there signals that we would that would indicate that again, the communication with host isn't great or this type of listing, if it's hosted by a person with multiple property?" I think there are factors we can be like, "Hey, we can learn this very explicit thing in a given period of time." (00:12:32): And you can do what I call unscalable things in that prototyping phase, in that early phase to go learn those lessons. But you just have to be very, very clear with your team on what phase you're in. "Hey, we're in the learning phase and we explicitly are trying to learn these things" versus, "Hey, we have this really big vision and we're just going to go at it." That is not recommended in my mind. It's breaking it down into these smaller chunks. That I think gets you the balance of thinking really, really big, but also being able to be like, "Okay, we are still going to be able to say, 'Okay, this path is not going to work out. We ran at it for a short period of time. We got these learnings, now let's go down this other path.'"
turns.zh:
我认为每个公司都必须拥有远大抱负，这一点至关重要。如果没有宏伟的愿景，创新将举步维艰，但同时必须将宏大愿景与精心策划的执行相结合。因此，我认为最重要的建议之一是，如何清晰界定当前所处的阶段？所以我觉得，在某个阶段明确目标是完全合理的。比如，“我们打算在未来六个月、三个月（或任何设定的时间段）内尝试X项目，并且明确致力于研究以下问题：用户为何会流失？是否存在某些信号表明房东沟通不畅，或者某类房源由多套房产的房东挂牌？”诸如此类问题，我们都能在特定时间段内进行深入探究。

（00:12:32）在原型阶段或早期阶段，你可以尝试那些不可扩展的创意方案，以此积累经验。但关键在于，要让团队清晰了解当前所处的阶段。“我们正处于学习阶段，明确致力于研究这些问题”，而非“我们怀揣着宏伟愿景，一味埋头苦干”。在我看来，这种做法不可取。将目标拆解成更小的阶段，能让你在保持远大格局的同时，灵活调整方向。当发现某条路径行不通时，及时止损，转向新方向，这才是明智之举。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's also some cost fallacy that kicks in of just like, "Oh, I spend so much time and money and resources on this thing. Let's just go a little bit longer. Let's just see if we give it another quarter, maybe it'll work out."
turns.zh: 是的，人们还常陷入一种成本误区，比如：“我已经在这件事上投入了大量时间、金钱和资源，再坚持一会儿看看吧。再给它一个季度时间，或许就能成功了。”

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: You should articulate what success looks like and the milestones you want to hit in the small intervals that I talked about. So you don't get into this world where you're like, "Hey, I've gone for two years investing in this thing. Now we got to cut it." It's like, what is the quarter long milestone? Okay, what's the next quarter long milestone? And every single point, what is a go and no-go? And I think that really can help a team and a company say "It's okay. I invested a quarter in it, but I didn't invest two years."
turns.zh: 你需要清晰界定成功的标准，并在上述提到的短期阶段设定明确的里程碑。这样就不会陷入“我已经在这件事上投入了两年时间，现在却不得不砍掉它”的困境。相反，要问自己：季度目标是什么？下一个季度目标又是什么？每个阶段的关键节点是什么？哪些是可以推进的，哪些必须停止？我认为这种做法能帮助团队和公司清醒地认识到：“投入一个季度没问题，但没必要投入两年。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other important lesson here is about the importance of as a product leader pushing back and convincing leadership that you are wrong and this shouldn't happen. I remember talking to one of our colleagues, Mike Lewis, who was leading a different team with Airbnb, and he was just like, "Oh, I realized I'm the person that should be saying, 'No, we shouldn't do this now'" because he was the head of product for one of the new [inaudible 00:14:09]. And I know maybe in that situation it was impossible because Brian was very into this and everyone was like, "We need to do this thing." (00:14:18): I guess is there anything you've learned about how to push back on these sorts of things that the founder's really into when it makes sense to go along? Like "Cool, let's do it. Let's buy in." As a leader, you have to be excited and he needs to feel like, "Oh, JZ is really excited about this too. We got to try it." Even though maybe you feel like it's not going to work out. So I guess the question is when do you think it makes sense to try convince the founder, "No, this is the bad idea" versus like "Let's go for it"?
turns.zh: 另一个重要的教训是，作为产品负责人，必须敢于反对并说服领导层，告诉他们自己的想法是错误的，这种做法不应继续下去。我记得曾与我们的同事Mike Lewis交谈，他当时在Airbnb负责另一个团队。他说道："哦，我意识到我应该说'不，我们现在不应该做这件事'。"因为他是Airbnb新项目的首席产品经理。我知道在那种情况下可能无解，因为Brian对此非常执着，每个人都说："我们必须要做这件事。"（00:14:18）我想问的是，当创始人非常热衷于某个想法时，你如何反对？比如"好吧，我们就这么做吧。我们买进吧。"作为领导者，你必须充满热情，让对方感觉"哦，JZ对此也很兴奋。我们得试试看。"即使你可能觉得这不会成功。所以我想问的是，当你认为有必要说服创始人"不，这是一个糟糕的主意"，而不是"我们就这么做吧"时，何时才是合适的时机？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think first it comes down to your conviction. Do you actually have conviction that this is a bad idea or are you personally still learning? Right. I think if you're at the point, if you're like, "I have total conviction," then your job is to say, no, you really... If you do not, you're not doing your job. And then the question is what are the tips in how to convince someone who's very bought into an idea that that's not the right idea? And there what I would say is it's understanding the spirit of what they're trying to achieve. Being able to go back with, "Hey, I understand the spirit. The spirit is that we're trying to get people who previously didn't consider Airbnb before to come and use Airbnb, but the right way to do it is not this very time-intensive, cost-intensive way to inspect all these homes. The way to do it is to be much more granular in what we ask people when they upload their home and more checks in that. And that could be automated and through technology as opposed to through humans." (00:15:37): It's coming back with actual options. It's like saying... And I think we did that a little bit to be honest, when we as a team evolve, we learn and we're like, "This isn't going to work." And I explicitly moved off the team and I was like, "I'm going to work on the review system. I'm going to continue to evolve this and make it better because that is the actual scalable way to do this as opposed to keep going at it in the very manual process." (00:15:59): And so I think that the biggest tip I would have for people in this situation is really understand whether it's the founder or your manager or whoever it is, what is it that they're trying to accomplish for the user and for the business? Remind them of that, get aligned on that. And then come back with better options. A lot of these people, they're very smart and they're very motivated. They ultimately want to just do the right thing for their users. When you come back with a much better solution and you have the data and you have the thinking behind it's very rare that someone will be like, "I still want to go after this solution despite the fact that it's not working and you proposed a much better path forward."
turns.zh: 我认为首先要看你的信念。你是否真的坚信这是一个糟糕的主意，还是你个人还在学习阶段？对。我认为如果你已经到了"我完全坚信"的地步，那么你的职责就是说不，你真的得这么做。如果你不这么做，就是失职。那么问题是，如何说服一个对某个想法深信不疑的人，让他们相信这不是正确的做法？我认为关键在于理解他们想要实现的目标。能够反驳道："嘿，我理解你的初衷。你的初衷是让那些之前从未考虑过Airbnb的人来使用Airbnb，但正确的做法不是用这种耗时耗力、成本高昂的方式去检查所有房源。正确的做法应该是更细致地询问用户上传房源时的信息，并加强审核。这些都可以通过自动化和技术手段实现，而不是靠人工操作。"（00:15:37）关键在于拿出切实可行的方案。比如我们团队在迭代过程中，就曾这样做过。我们意识到某个方案行不通，就明确退出团队，转而专注于开发评论系统，不断优化它，因为这才是可扩展的正确路径，而不是继续采用非常手动化的流程。（00:15:59）所以我认为对于处于这种情况的人，最重要的建议就是真正理解对方——无论是创始人、经理还是其他人——他们想为用户和业务实现什么目标？提醒他们这一点，并达成共识。然后拿出更好的方案。这些人通常都很聪明、很有上进心，他们最终都想为用户做正确的事。当你拿出更好的解决方案，数据和思路都摆在面前时，很少有人会说："尽管这个方案行不通，但我还是想继续推行它，而你提出的路径要好得多。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think to touch on what you've already said is also make sure it's actually... There's a world where this could work. Do some math to figure out if this is a business that will actually make some money in the future.
turns.zh: 接下来，我想再谈谈你之前提到的观点，那就是要确保产品实际上……确实有成功的可能。可以算一笔账，看看这个业务未来能否真正盈利。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm going to bounce around a little bit. I have a bunch of different questions around different topics. You popularized this concept of minimal lovable product versus this idea that everyone always comes back to, which is minimal viable product. Can you just talk about what is a minimal lovable product and then when does it make sense to go in that direction versus a traditional MVP?
turns.zh: 好的。我接下来要多聊几点。关于不同主题，我有一堆问题。你推广了最小可爱产品（Minimal Lovable Product）这个概念，而传统的MVP（最小可行产品）是大家常提到的概念。你能否先讲讲什么是最小可爱产品，然后再讲什么时候该选择这种方向，而非传统的MVP？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: The reason I care so much about minimal lovable product is because I do think in a world where there are so many different options, it's hard to just feel like, "Hey, use this thing. It barely meets a quality bar." And so I think this idea of actually deeply understanding for the thing that you're working on, what is a lovable experience? What is the quality bar that resonates with your users? And again, especially in a world where there might be a lot of different options. Minimal lovable products is the new MVP. The new minimal viable product. (00:17:40): So I think that's the real point, but at the end of the day, it does come back to what are the options that a user has and what are they trying to do? So there's a world where your quality bar, your "Quality bar," or let's call it your polished bar, can be a little bit lower because the reality is the thing that you're "Competing against" or you're replacing is literally a manual workflow. It's like spreadsheets. It's doing something in a super terrible way. (00:18:05): So you want to get your product to market as quickly as possible, so it doesn't make sense for you to be like, "I'm going to build these 15 additional features." Because compared to what people are doing right now, your product without those 15 additional features is perfectly fine, perfectly usable, and perfectly quite honestly lovable. So it requires a lot of understanding of, again, your users and the space that you play in and the tolerance of your given user. So for example, a designer might have a lot higher of a bar of like "This is the kind of workflow I want, this is the kind of bar for my product." But again, someone sitting on the finance team or the IT team, their bar might be like, "Oh, I'm used to doing these 15 things and so your thing is just a lot better."
turns.zh: 我之所以如此关注最小可爱产品，是因为在有众多选择的世界里，用户很难会觉得“嘿，用这个产品吧，它勉强达到质量标准”。所以我认为，要深入理解你正在开发的产品，什么样的体验才是可爱的？什么样的质量标准才能真正打动用户？尤其是在有众多选择的环境下，最小可爱产品是新的MVP，新的最小可行产品。（00:17:40）所以我认为这才是关键，但归根结底，还是要看用户有哪些选择，他们的需求是什么？在某些情况下，你的质量标准、所谓的“完美标准”可以稍低一些，因为现实情况是，你所“竞争”的对象或者你要替代的产品，可能只是手动流程。比如电子表格。用户用着那种极差的体验。所以你要尽快将产品推向市场，所以没必要去添加15个额外功能。因为相较于用户当前使用的产品，没有这15个功能的你的产品已经足够好、足够易用、足够讨喜了。这需要你深入理解用户、所在的行业，以及用户的容忍度。比如设计师可能对“我想要这样的工作流程”有更高的要求，但IT团队或财务团队的人可能觉得“哦，我习惯做这15件事，而你的产品好多了”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to go even one level deeper. Is there an example of something you've worked on that was minimal lovable product that you think about? Or is there something out there that's an example of here's maybe an example of a minimal lovable product versus MVP?
turns.zh: 我想再深入探讨一下。你有没有做过的最小可爱产品案例值得分享？或者有没有其他案例能对比最小可爱产品和MVP？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Again, it's very hard. I think every product team, every product person struggles with this idea of what is the minimal viable. Even that concept itself is difficult and not to mention minimal lovable. I'll give a Webflow example. Very recently, so have been investing in a couple of new features, memberships and logic, new functionality for our users. And what we realized at the end of the day after investing in these areas, we were like, "Hey, we can get to minimal viable, but we don't know if we can actually get to minimal lovable in a way that our users really, really want. And so does it make sense for us to continue to go down this path of continues to chip away to get to minimal lovable when we are maybe hitting diminishing returns for our user base? Or does it actually make sense to release what we have but then encourage our ecosystem to contribute the lovable piece?" (00:19:56): And again, it's not just like you put it out there and you hope, you have to have a very strong point of view of are we at minimal viable, are we at minimal lovable? Where in between are we? And so having that point of view and then being able to say, "Are we going to be able to meet it as a company? Are we going to rely on our ecosystem to help us meet it? What are we actually going to do?" And then even within the feature set, it's very much a how do we do some things well as opposed to do a little bit of everything? I think that is a big piece of minimal lovable, which is again... To me it's better to do five things instead of the 15 things in a really, really great way with a high degree of polish with a, "Oh, this really meets my need," versus trying to do everything and just doing a little bit of everything. And so every part of the experience feels a little bit clunky. It's not quite there. (00:20:45): People I think would actually respect this idea of "You've given me minimal lovable in five areas as opposed to minimal viable in 15 areas."
turns.zh:
再次强调，这真的很难。我认为每个产品团队、每个产品经理都在为"最小可行产品"的概念而纠结。甚至这个概念本身就很困难，更别提"最小可爱产品"了。我举个Webflow的例子。最近，我们一直在投入精力开发新功能，比如会员制和逻辑规则，提升用户体验。但在投入这些资源后，我们最终意识到："虽然我们能达到最小可行产品标准，但不确定能否真正实现用户真正想要的'最小可爱产品'。那么，继续沿着这条路走下去，不断完善'最小可爱产品'，直到用户满意，是否值得呢？还是直接发布现有功能，然后鼓励生态系统共同完善'可爱'部分？"（00:19:56）  
再说一次，这不只是把产品推出来然后祈祷成功。你必须有清晰的判断：我们现在处于最小可行阶段，还是最小可爱阶段？两者之间处于什么位置？有了这样的认知后，你才能决定："作为公司，我们能否达成目标？还是要依靠生态系统共同完成？我们到底该怎么做？"  
即使在功能集设计上，关键在于如何把某些功能做得精益求精，而不是面面俱到。我认为这正是"最小可爱产品"的核心所在。对我来说，宁愿把五个功能做到极致，带来高度精良的体验，让用户感叹"这正是我需要的"，也不愿把15个功能都浅尝辄止，导致用户体验生硬。（00:20:45）  
我相信用户会更认可这样的理念："你只在五个方面提供了最小可爱产品，而不是在15个方面追求最小可行产品。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you've seen of just that makes something lovable? I don't know. I know it's not easy to define, but what are things you've seen that makes something lovable? Is it delightful features? Or is it what you're saying, which is just things are actually good, there's fewer things, but they're each really good?
turns.zh: 有没有什么具体案例能体现出产品的"可爱"特质？我不知道。这确实很难定义，但你见过哪些能让产品变得"可爱的"例子？是令人愉悦的功能？还是你所说的"简洁但优质"的理念？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: There's definitely this idea of the thing is just good. It has all. High quality, it's not janky, it doesn't feel weird. I'll give you a very small example again, just from Webflow, this idea of keyboard shortcuts, feels small, but that is a piece that creates a lot of love from user base who are power users. And then there's this concept of pixie dusts, and maybe I'll pull out of call it like design tool space and we'll talk about some of the other things, whether it's Dropbox or Airbnb, but you can just do a little bit of that extra pixie dusts. So an example from Airbnb when we're doing the mobile app revamp where like "There's like these basic table stakes, but if we actually added in templates and we made it so that these templates could be maybe pre-populated in certain ways from the content they already have," that is lovable, that is that extra little bit of pixie dust and spending the time to do that. (00:21:55): Again, you can't pixie dust everything. At the end of the day, you basically have your time, your staffing and the scope of your project and something has to give. And so at the end of the day, you can't just keep investing, keep investing because it's going to push out your launch timeline, but can you pick a few different areas where you're like, "I'm going to scatter that pixie dust, I'm going to do a little bit more than what users are expecting"? And that creates that lovability.
turns.zh:
确实有这样一种理念——这个产品就是好的。它具备一切优点：高品质、操作流畅、体验自然。我再举个小例子，还是来自 Webflow。键盘快捷键这个功能看似微不足道，但它却深受高级用户的喜爱。还有“魔法粉尘”（pixie dusts）这个概念，或许我可以把它延伸到整个设计工具领域，再谈谈其他案例，比如 Dropbox 或 Airbnb。关键在于在产品中注入那些额外的“魔法粉尘”。以 Airbnb 的移动应用改版为例，我们原本只做了基本的优化，但当我们加入模板功能，并让这些模板能根据已有内容进行预填充时，用户反响热烈。这就是所谓的「魔法粉尘」，投入额外精力就能创造惊喜。

（00:21:55）当然，并非所有地方都能添加「魔法粉尘」。最终你必须权衡时间、人力和项目规模，必然会有取舍。不能为了追求完美而无限延期，但你可以挑选几个关键点，比如“我要在用户预期之上再增添一些惊喜”。这样才能真正提升产品的亲和力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shifting to a different topic, I know you have strong opinions about road mapping and OKRs, improvisation, and I know that's a big topic, but let me just ask, what's the most common advice you give around how to roadmap well, do OKRs, prioritize and/or just, I don't know, common mantras or things you always come back to be successful in these areas?
turns.zh: 转到另一个话题，我知道你对路线图规划和 OKR（目标与关键结果）、即兴发挥等理念有独到见解。这都是复杂的课题，但我想问问，在路线图规划、OKR执行、优先级排序方面，你最常给出的建议是什么？或者说，有哪些通用的方法论或成功秘诀是你反复强调的？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Road mapping prioritization are one bucket for me. And then OKRs is another. So I'll maybe give you my biggest tip in each one of these buckets. (00:22:46): So for road mapping, my biggest thing that I tell my teams is "You're telling a story. So what I want from you is I want themes, I want a story. Why are these things the biggest things to invest in these levers, the biggest ones to pull?" And what I really don't want, what I think is a very common mistake from road mapping is people thinking a spreadsheet with a bunch of projects, the RICE framework, everything has an impact, a cost and an effort column filled out. They think that is prioritization and that is a roadmap. If you just do that right and then you present that to your team, they're off to the races. (00:23:26): But what people, what humans really crave is like, "Why am I doing this body of work?" And I think it's also really, really important to have that really crisply articulated in your own head because ultimately what happens is you'll learn things as a product person. You'll be like, "Oh, I assumed this in the narrative in my head about my users or about my product area, and then I learned why and therefore my thinking changed." So instead of it being this massive spreadsheet where you're going in, you're tweaking all the values, what is the story that you're telling about your roadmap that these inputs can then go and influence? (00:23:59): It could be like, "Hey, I just realized I didn't know before that we have a lot more power users on our," or "Maybe we have a lot more non-technical users." That input changes my roadmap and changes my themes in a pretty dramatic way. So skating at that level is really, really critical, I think for a roadmap as opposed to going down to the really granular details of the how. So that's the biggest thing on road mapping, which is like tell a story. What are your themes? Make it so that your team can come up with the actual how and the projects and all the little details, but really create that scaffolding for them to know what's important.
turns.zh: 对我来说，路线图优先级排序是一个重点领域。OKRs 则是另一个重点领域。所以，我可能会在每个领域里给出我最重要的建议。（00:22:46）：对于路线图规划，我给团队最重要的建议是：“你们是在讲一个故事。所以我希望你们能提供主题和故事框架。为什么这些事物是值得投资的重点？哪些杠杆最值得拉动？” 我最不希望看到的，也是路线图规划中一个很常见的错误，就是人们以为只要填好一个包含项目列表的电子表格，应用 RICE 框架，填满影响、成本和投入三列，就完成了优先级排序和路线图规划。这样做根本不算优先级排序，也不算真正的路线图。如果你能正确完成这些步骤，再向团队展示，他们就会全力推进了。（00:23:26）：但人们真正渴望的，是能听到这样的问题：“我为什么要做这项工作？” 我认为，在自己脑海中清晰地阐明这个问题至关重要。毕竟，作为产品从业者，你会不断学习新知识。比如，你可能会发现：“哦，我之前在脑海中构建的用户画像或产品领域假设有误，现在我知道了原因，思维也因此发生了转变。” 所以，优先级排序不应只是一个庞大的电子表格，你需要不断调整各项数据。关键在于，你要讲述一个清晰的故事，让这些输入数据能真正影响到路线图的规划。（00:23:59）：比如，“嘿，我刚意识到我们的超级用户数量远超预期”，或者“或许非技术用户的比例比我们预想的要高得多”。这些洞察会极大地改变路线图的规划和主题设定。因此，站在宏观层面思考路线图规划至关重要，而不是深究具体细节。这就是路线图规划最重要的要点：讲述一个引人入胜的故事。你的主题是什么？要让团队能基于这些主题制定具体的实施方案和项目计划，但首先要为他们搭建一个清晰的框架，让他们明白什么才是最重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can I ask a follow-up question on that?
turns.zh: 我能就此提个后续问题吗？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Totally, yeah.
turns.zh: 当然可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's easy to visualize the roadmap of a spreadsheet to help people visualize what you're suggesting there. What does that actual artifact look like? Is it a doc with maybe an ancillary spreadsheet of the actual prioritization? Is it a deck? How do you actually deliver this to you with like "JZ, here's our proposal for our team"?
turns.zh: 用电子表格直观呈现路线图，能帮助人们更好地理解你的建议。具体的成果应该是什么样子的？是包含优先级排序的附带文档？还是演示文稿？你如何把这些成果交付给团队，比如说：“JZ，这是我们团队的提案。”

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Yeah, I'm a big fan of docs and decks are obviously helpful if you're talking live, but I do think in a remote-first culture or lots of us are in hybrid remote cultures it's hard because decks typically require a voiceover. And so we have been doing a big push even on my teams where I'm like, "Write it down and document. Force yourself to write the pros because when you write the pros, you can actually add that level of granularity." So very much so the same way like "I'm a roadmap is a story. You're telling themes, you write a story in a notebook, you write a story on pages," and so a doc is definitely preferred. And even in the doc just being like, "Here's what we're trying to achieve, here are the big areas I want to invest in, here are my big themes." And then going into each of those themes and being like, "These are the big projects." (00:25:40): And then linking out, again, not even to a spreadsheet, but linking out to the artifacts and the systems that your team actually uses. So if your team uses Jira, go ahead and link out to Jira because so often docs get out of... Or spreadsheets get out of date, because they're like a snapshot of whatever it is that you needed at that point in time. But instead you link out to the actual things that your teams are working out of, you can always be like, "These are the themes. I will edit these if I learn major things that would change my themes. And then let's go link out to the Jira where you can just see the snapshot of the roadmap at any given point in time."
turns.zh: 是的，我非常推崇文档和演示文稿，但如果是现场演示，演示文稿显然很有帮助。不过在远程优先的文化中（或者像我们许多人所处的混合远程文化中），情况就比较复杂了，因为演示文稿通常需要配音讲解。因此，我们一直在大力推广——即使在我的团队中，我也会说：“把想法写下来，做好记录。强迫自己列出优点，因为当你写下优点时，就能增添更多细节。”这和「路线图就是一个故事」的理念如出一辙——你要讲述主题，在笔记本上写下故事，在页面上勾勒故事。所以文档绝对是首选。即使在文档中，你也可以写道：「这是我们要达成的目标」、「这是我想投入精力的关键领域」、「这些是我的核心主题」。然后再深入每个主题，写道：「这些是重大项目」。（00:25:40）接着再添加链接，甚至不需要链接到电子表格，而是链接到团队实际使用的工件和系统。比如，如果团队使用Jira，就直接链接到Jira，因为文档和电子表格往往会过时——它们只是某个时间点所需信息的快照。但如果你链接到团队实际使用的工具，用户就能看到路线图的实时更新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a template or common structure you suggest to teams for laying out this story or is it just depends on the quarter, it depends on the year?
turns.zh: 你有没有建议团队用于规划这个故事的模板或通用结构，还是说这取决于季度或年度计划？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I'll give a plug for a new thing coming out of Reforge, which is this concept of artifacts. And so we do have a lot of artifacts out there, so what's our general product development process? What are our templates for our specs? What are our templates for some of these things that we're talking about, a roadmap, like a broader roadmap instead of just a feature spec. So yes, we have a ton of those artifacts, are always evolving. I think every team takes it and tweaks it a little bit, but I'm a big believer of bringing those artifacts back and then sharing them across the team. And so product operations is also a function that we've invested in because it just really greases the wheels, gets all of our teams speaking the same language.
turns.zh: 我要为Reforge即将推出的新功能打个广告，那就是工件概念。我们确实有大量工件，比如产品开发流程模板、规格模板，以及我们讨论的路线图等内容——而不仅仅是单个功能的规格模板。所以是的，我们有大量这类工件，并且它们在不断演进。我认为每个团队都会根据实际情况进行调整，但我非常支持将这些工件标准化并在团队中共享。产品运营团队也是我们重点投入的部门，因为它能有效协调各团队的沟通，保证大家用同一种语言交流。
