turns.zh: 太棒了。（00:26:59）：本期节目由Superhuman赞助。你们每天花多少时间处理邮件？团队成员呢？你可能没有意识到，但你的邮件工具正在浪费你的时间。Superhuman专为高效团队打造的极速邮件工具，与Gmail和Outlook兼容。使用Superhuman的团队每天花费一半时间处理邮件，回复邮件数量增加两倍，每周节省超过四小时的工作时间。这样算下来，每年能节省一个多月的宝贵时间。通过Superhuman，你可以将收件箱分为VIP、团队成员和喜爱产品邮件三大类，减少切换上下文的烦恼，确保重要邮件不会遗漏。若未收到回复，你还能设置提醒，及时跟进邮件沟通。借助智能写作、编辑、摘要生成和翻译等强大AI功能，你将工作效率提升至新高度。加入最高效团队行列，释放超人般的生产力。在superhuman.com/lenny可免费试用一个月。就是superhuman.com/lenny。（00:28:02）：接下来转换话题。对于希望加速职业发展的初级产品经理，你最重要的建议是什么？你发现他们最常遇到的阻碍或瓶颈是什么？或者说，有哪些可改变的因素能助力他们加速成长？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: There's so many parts to it, but I'll pick one. And there are many frameworks even beyond the one, but let's pick one for your question, which is I think it's really important to become really good at and also known for something. And what I mean by that is when you're known in your company for a particular thing.... I'll give you a couple examples. You could be known for shepherding the most complex launches because you're just so good at quarterbacking, working with go-to market teams and cross-functional stakeholders, that could be your thing. You could be known for working on the most technically complex problems. You could be known for working on things that are really regulatory complex. Find something that you can be really, really good at. And the reason I give that advice is because when you do that, you can crush the projects that you get. Because you're making a name for yourself, reputation, and then you are giving more responsibility. People tend to flock and give responsibility to the people that are known for being excellent at something.
turns.zh: 这方面有太多可说的，但我会挑选一个要点。即使不止一个框架，但针对你的问题，我们可以选一个。我认为真正精通并以某项技能闻名至关重要。我的意思是，当你在公司因某项特长而闻名时……我举几个例子。你可能因成功领导最复杂的项目而闻名，因为你擅长统筹工作，与市场团队和跨职能利益相关者合作，这就是你的专长。你可能因解决最具技术挑战的问题而闻名。你可能因处理监管复杂性极高的问题而闻名。找到你真正擅长的东西。我给出这个建议的原因是，当你做到这一点时，你就能出色完成接手的项目。因为你为自己树立了声誉，获得了更多责任。人们往往会追随并将责任赋予那些以某项专长闻名的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something you were known to be excellent at in the course of your career?
turns.zh: 在你的职业生涯中，有没有你擅长且闻名于世的技能？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I would say early on in my career, it was actually the fact that I had a strong analytics background. And so when I joined gaming, I came from consulting, I didn't have any CS background or design background, and so it was really creating a reputation around being very analytical, around being able to analyze the datasets of my game and then make decisions. I also learned as I was doing that I was actually really good at execution, and so being able to keep a lot of plates spinning and working on the largest studio and managing all the complex pieces of that, that was what I discovered. I didn't know this, but I discovered as I started working in the role. (00:29:58): And so that was something I brought to Dropbox. When I joined Dropbox. It was like I knew that I could work with a lot of different teams and make sure that we hit a launch deadline, and so I would find myself trying to lean into that superpower and then when delivering upon that, getting more responsibility, "Hey, you just launched this really complex thing, this was a project that had to work across a lot of different platforms. We're using Griddle APIs." And it was a very, very small team and it had a very, very tight deadline. (00:30:29): So when you're like, "I can do something like this," you end up getting more responsibility because people were like, "Oh, she was able to do something that was really hard with a small team," and so that's how you get more responsibility. But it has evolved in my career. I think that at the beginning of your career, you do want to lean into some of these pieces. It makes sense, but also even when you start to manage, it shifts dramatically. Being known as the best executor is not necessarily the thing that gives you and your team the most responsibility. So as I've grown my career, whether it's at Airbnb or WeWork or other places I flex into maybe a different... It's like taking your core strength but then flexing it and finding different ways to bring it to life.
turns.zh: 我得说，在我职业生涯早期，最关键的优势其实是拥有强大的分析能力。当我转入游戏行业时，我来自咨询行业，没有任何计算机科学或设计背景。因此，我通过在游戏数据分析方面的出色表现，逐步树立了严谨分析的声誉，能够解析游戏数据集并做出决策。在此过程中，我发现自己其实很擅长执行任务——能够同时处理多项工作，管理大型工作室的复杂事务。这也是我在担任现职后才意识到的。（00:29:58）这也是我带入Dropbox的能力。当我加入Dropbox时，我深知自己能与多个团队协作，确保产品按时上线。因此，我会努力发挥这种专长，而当我成功交付项目后，便获得了更多责任。比如，"你刚刚上线了这个复杂的功能，这个项目需要跨多个平台运行，我们还用到了Griddle API。"当时团队规模很小，时间极其紧迫。（00:30:29）当你展现出"能完成这样的任务"时，人们会赋予你更多责任，因为他们会想："她能在小团队中完成如此艰巨的任务。"这就是获得更多责任的秘诀。但这种模式在我的职业生涯中不断演变。我认为，在职业生涯初期，你确实需要专注于某些领域，这很合理，但当你开始管理团队时，情况会发生巨大转变。被视为最出色的执行者并不一定能为你和团队赢得最多责任。因此，随着职业生涯的发展，无论是在Airbnb、WeWork还是其他公司，我都会灵活运用核心优势，寻找不同方式将其发挥出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Much of what I just heard is you just worked incredibly hard and just got shit done. And I think that's very, very important and often leads to a lot of success.
turns.zh: 我刚听到的大部分内容都是你非常努力地完成任务。我认为这非常重要，往往能带来巨大成功。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: PMs have to get shit done. Yeah, ultimately you're responsible for the outcome just no matter what happens.
turns.zh: 产品经理必须把事情做好。是的，无论发生什么，最终的责任都在你身上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I like that. Be known for getting shit done and working really hard, and that's never going to serve you badly. I think that is just lasting advice for being successful as a PM. I realized that we were talking about your tips on prioritization, road mapping and then OKRs, and then I shifted topics and you never got to the OKR bucket. So let me come back to that.
turns.zh: 是的，我赞同这一点。以能把事情做好、努力工作而闻名，这永远不会让你吃亏。我认为这就是作为产品经理成功的永恒秘诀。我意识到我们之前讨论的是你关于优先级排序、路线图和OKRs的建议，然后话题转换了，你一直没提到OKRs。所以让我再回过头来谈谈这个。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Yes. My biggest tip on OKRs is actually get really, really crisp on qualitatively. What would make you say "Yes, we did a great job"? And the reason I pushed so hard on that is because I see so many teams get really mucked down by OKRs. They're like, "Oh man, if I don't hit my OKR, I feel like I'm going to have a really bad reputation, or maybe I won't get promoted." You just get all this fear around OKRs. And so you see people, you see people sandbagging, you see people being hesitant to put in numbers until the very last second until they're super, super confident. And that results in ultimately a failure for your company to innovate and move quickly. (00:32:29): And so what I really push on for OKRs is are you actually... What's the spirit... I think I asked this question maybe too much to my team, but what is the spirit of what you're trying to achieve and what would make you say, 'I really, really crushed it this past quarter'? And so it's less about I would rather have all the OKRs be red or yellow and we missed everything and we learned around why we missed it than everything to be green. In fact, when everything's green, you're like, "We definitely did not set ambitious enough OKRs." And so it really pushed a lot on what does it truly mean to crush it and be successful? What does it mean for our users? What does it mean for our business? What does that... For our users to feel X, can you describe that? Can you write that out? For our business to see this in terms of the revenue growth? (00:33:17): And I think it's really hard because a lot of times, you get your data scientists, you get the PM themselves being like, "Oh man, I'm owning an input metric, not an output metric. And so I definitely can't sign up for that revenue target because I have an input metric." And all of those things are true, but if you don't do the homework of really drawing that line of being like, "This is the ultimate thing I want to do for the company and for my users," then a lot of times you end up hitting all your OKRs, but the company and your users at large are like, "I don't feel anything different." Your company doesn't look at the things that you've worked on and they don't say like "This is a smashing success." Your users are feeling no differently. And so that is the worst outcome in my head where your OKRs, you're almost like doing OKRs for the sake of OKRs, as opposed to letting them be a guide to delivering really great product to your end customer.
turns.zh: 是的。关于OKR，我最重要的建议其实是，在定性方面要做到非常、非常清晰。什么样的情况会让你觉得“是的，我们做得非常出色”？我之所以如此强调这一点，是因为我看到很多团队被OKR搞得焦头烂额。他们会想：“天哪，如果达不到OKR目标，我感觉自己的声誉会受损，或者可能升不了职。”人们对OKR充满恐惧。于是你会看到人们藏着掖着，不愿过早设定目标，非要等到最后一刻才勉强填写数据。这最终会导致公司创新和快速发展失败。（00:32:29）所以我对OKR真正强调的是：你们是否真正……你们的精神核心是什么？我可能对团队问过太多次这个问题，但你们到底想达成什么目标？什么情况下你们会觉得“上个季度我们真的超额完成了任务”？关键不在于所有OKR都是红色或黄色然后大家都达不到目标，而是要总结失败原因。事实上，当所有OKR都是绿色时，你会觉得“我们设定的OKR目标太不具挑战性了”。所以真正的问题在于：什么才算真正成功？对用户意味着什么？对业务意味着什么？用户的感受是什么？你能具体描述吗？你能量化成数据吗？对业务而言，收入增长情况如何？（00:33:17）我觉得这很难，因为很多时候，数据科学家和产品经理会说：“哦，我负责的是输入指标，不是输出指标。所以我肯定没法签下那个收入目标。”这些说法都有道理，但如果你不认真思考：这是我想为公司和用户做的最重要的事吗？那么很多时候你可能达成了所有OKR，但公司和用户却毫无感觉。公司不会认为你做了很棒的工作，而用户也感受不到变化。这才是最糟糕的结果——你只是为了完成OKR而完成OKR，而不是让OKR成为交付优质产品的指南。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like the idea of that, but imagine what often happens is you sign up for an ambitious OKR, you don't wait till the last second to commit to it and then ends up being red, and then you go into performance reviews and like, "Oh, Lenny didn't hit his OKRs. Look at this guy. His team is not doing great." How do you think about that as a product leader understanding if the team actually did well and the PM is performing well when they sign up for these really ambitious OKRs and their story's great and they're doing the right thing, but they fail?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个理念，但想象一下常见的情况：你设定了一个雄心勃勃的OKR，不等到最后一刻才承诺达成，结果最后还是红色。然后绩效评估时就会说：“哦，莱尼没达成OKR。看看这个人，他们团队表现不佳。”作为产品负责人，当团队设定了非常高远的OKR，故事听起来很棒，方向也正确，但最终失败了，你如何判断团队是否真的表现出色？PM是否真的在努力？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: First of all, I think it's creating a culture where you are not punished for that. Because I definitely don't want a culture where it's like you took a risk and you failed and therefore your performance is impacted. I'd much rather people take risks than to be safe. So I think that's the first thing. That being said, you're also not doing a good job as a PM if you're like, "This is my super, super ambitious thing," and you're like, "I have no idea how to achieve it." Your job is to dream big and also have a plan to go tackle it. And so what I would expect the PM to be able to say is, "This is my North Star. I'm not going to be able to do that in a quarter, that just is unreasonable, but here are the five milestones," whatever number, some number of milestones "That it's going to take me to do quarter over quarter to achieve this really, really ambitious thing. And let me draw you that path. Here's the milestone all the way across, and this is the first one. This is why it's so meaningful." (00:35:24): So I expect that combination where you're like, "I know where I'm going. It's really, really ambitious." And then you can then break it down. But again, I would much rather have someone shoot for the moon, even for someone to say like "This is the thing I really want to do. I don't know my path yet" than to be really, really safe. Because when you're safe, you're always going to be building something suboptimal. It's going to be suboptimal use of your resources as opposed to actually trying to figure out what the best swing that you can take is.
turns.zh: 首先，我认为我们需要营造一种不因冒险而受到惩罚的文化。因为我绝对不希望在一个组织中，人们因为冒险失败而导致业绩受损。我更希望人们勇于尝试，而非墨守成规。所以这才是首要之务。话虽如此，如果作为产品经理，你只是说：“这是我一个超级雄心勃勃的想法”，而自己却毫无实现的思路，那你就没有做好自己的本职工作。你的职责是既要敢于畅想宏伟蓝图，又要制定切实可行的行动计划。因此，我期待产品经理能这样说：“这是我们的北极星目标。我知道季度内无法达成，但这些里程碑足以让我在逐季推进中逐步实现这个极具挑战性的目标。让我为你描绘这条路径。从这里到那里，每个节点都是里程碑，这是第一个。正因如此，这个目标才意义非凡。” （00:35:24） 因此，关键在于你要明确目标，说：“我知道自己要去哪里，虽然目标极具挑战性，但我会分解它。” 但我更希望看到人们敢于挑战极限，哪怕他们只是说：“这是我想做的事，目前还没有路径”，也比墨守成规要好得多。因为墨守成规意味着资源的低效利用，而非去探索最佳突破点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it sounds like it comes back to the story of the roadmap and what they're trying to accomplish, and just as long as it feels like the story made sense, there's a path there. The team did their best, I think we know it was really ambitious. We kind of knew maybe they wouldn't get there. It sounds like that's kind of the thing you look for in a performance of the PM.
turns.zh: 看来这又回到了路线图的故事和他们试图达成的目标上。只要这个故事逻辑清晰，就能找到路径。团队已经尽力了，我想我们都知道这个目标确实雄心勃勃。我们预料到他们可能无法达成。但这似乎正是衡量产品经理表现的标准。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Totally. Yeah.
turns.zh: 完全正确。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I mentioned WeWork and I want to spend a little time on WeWork. You were at WeWork for about a year, and I think it was in the middle of a lot of the craziness that went on at WeWork.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我提到了WeWork，想花点时间聊聊WeWork。你在WeWork待了大约一年，当时正值WeWork陷入诸多混乱之际。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: It was. It was 2019, I feel like that year it was either headlines were either about Trump or about WeWork in the news.
turns.zh: 确实如此。2019年，我感觉那一年新闻头条不是关于特朗普，就是关于WeWork。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's tough. So what was that like being a PM leader at a company in that craziness? And is there a takeaway from that experience that helps you be a better product manager, a leader, person?
turns.zh: 这确实很艰难。那么，在这种混乱的环境中担任产品经理领导者是怎样的体验？从这段经历中，你是否获得了有助于成为更优秀的产品经理、领导者或个人的启发？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Yeah, I learned a lot from my time there. I think the most important lesson I learned was really around... I think there's like a people leader management lesson, and then there's also just like a how do you build an org period. The people lesson I learned was just really around empathy. In fact, essentially what I was doing was I built a team. I spent the first six months of my time there actually growing my team a lot, and not just in the US but in Asia and in Europe. And then the second half of my time there was actually being like, "What do we do? If this is what's happening with WeWork, what are we actually going to do with all of these people who have come to WeWork to work?" (00:37:19): And there was so many lessons there around leadership, around how do you think about people? How do you think about giving them the right transition plans? It was a lot of learning. And I think probably a lot of people, even right now through the macroeconomic downturn, they're learning that lesson in a really hard way. And so it was definitely something that I got a crash course on, I think early. (00:37:44): And the second lesson really was around not over-hiring. And so I think that was huge, and I think I personally learned that lesson through my time there. And it's something that I'm very conscious of at any company that I go to. Just because laying off half your team is a terrible feeling. Literally having hired people and then having to let them go, it's not something you want to do. And so being really thoughtful around how do we not over-hire? How are we really clear about, again, these milestones of we got to get through these gates, we got to be able to show these types of results, and then we unlock hiring in X, Y, Z ways? That hygiene is really, really important.
turns.zh: 是啊，在那里工作的经历让我收获颇丰。我认为最重要的收获在于……首先是关于人员管理的课程，其次是如何构建一个组织架构。关于人员管理的部分，主要在于培养同理心。事实上，我当时的工作重点就是组建团队。入职的前六个月，我大力扩充了团队成员，不仅在美国本土，还在亚洲和欧洲地区招募人才。后半段工作则不得不面对一个严峻的现实：面对WeWork面临的困境，我们该如何安置这些前来工作的员工？（00:37:19）这段经历让我深刻领悟了领导力的真谛，学会了如何善待员工，为他们制定合理的过渡计划。整个过程让我收获良多。我相信，即使在当下宏观经济低迷的环境下，许多人也在以惨痛的方式领悟着这些教训。而我早早接触到了这些挑战，无疑是接受了一次速成课程。（00:37:44）第二个重要经验是关于避免过度招聘。这对公司至关重要，我在WeWork的经历让我深刻认识到这一点。在加入任何新公司时，我都会格外谨慎地思考如何避免过度招聘。毕竟裁掉一半团队成员的滋味实在不好受，明明才刚招来新人，却又不得不让他们走人，这种感觉太痛苦了。因此，必须制定清晰的招聘策略：在达成关键节点、取得预期成果后，再逐步放开招聘渠道。这套体系的规范性建设至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Feels like this connects back to the Airbnb Plus story of "Let's just be really ambitious. We don't have any idea how we're going to get there, but we're just going to go for it, hire like crazy, scale, put a lot of investment in this thing and hopefully we'll figure it out."
turns.zh: 这让我联想到Airbnb Plus的故事——“我们要怀揣远大抱负，尽管尚不清楚如何达成目标，但我们必须勇往直前，疯狂招人，大规模扩张，投入大量资源，希望最终能找到出路。”

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I do think there was a little bit of that in the ethos of how WeWork was functioning, for sure. I think that what was really important for us to do was to be like, "We have this." Operationally, WeWork is really strong. In fact, I went to WeWork because having been at Airbnb, I was like, "I don't feel like we've dialed this operational muscle down," but I know from what I've seen and the way WeWork has expanded, that they're really, really excellent at the operations. But I think it was, again, we hired beyond our skis on the tech side. It's like we don't need a team of this size to go do the things that are needed for the product to feel really great. At the end of the day, it's about booking. And yes, there's technology that would accelerate that, but do we need it to be super platform aware? Do we need it to be super futuristic? That's actually not what people care about. (00:39:19): So this all goes back to what are people's core desires in whatever product that they're using, whatever thing that your business is trying to serve them? And so really understanding that will help you have a sense of, "Hey, you can still be really ambitious." Again, in a hybrid world, it's like why have real dedicated office space? Every company could go through WeWork as opposed to this dedicated space. That's still a really good idea, that's still a really big vision and a relevant vision, but what's the key piece of that vision? The key piece of that vision is around inventory, and then you make that inventory management easier. You make all of these things easier, but that's not a technology play in the same way as it is an operational play. So just really understanding, again, you can still dream really big, but you don't have to dream big and hire big in all the things in order to have a very ambitious vision that you deliver to the market.
turns.zh: 我确实认为WeWork的运营理念中存在这样的倾向，这一点毋庸置疑。对我们而言，最重要的是要意识到：“我们拥有这些资源。”从运营角度看，WeWork确实非常出色。事实上，我之所以选择加入WeWork，是因为在Airbnb工作过后，我曾想：“我们似乎并没有充分发挥出运营方面的优势。”但从我观察到的WeWork扩张情况来看，他们在运营层面的表现确实堪称卓越。不过，我认为WeWork在技术团队的扩张上有些过度了。换句话说，要让产品体验真正出色，并不需要如此庞大的技术团队。归根结底，预订服务才是核心。诚然，技术可以加速这一进程，但我们真的需要过度依赖平台适配吗？真的需要追求极致的未来感吗？但这些其实并非用户真正关心的点。（00:39:19）所以，这一切都回归到用户对所使用产品的核心需求，以及你的业务试图满足的用户需求上。真正理解这些需求，才能让你明白：“嘿，你依然可以保持雄心壮志。” 在混合办公模式下，比如为什么要保留专属办公空间？每家公司都可以选择WeWork而非专属空间。这依然是个极具前瞻性的构想，但关键在于库存管理。通过简化库存管理，你能让整个系统更高效。这并非技术层面的创新，而是运营策略的优化。因此，要想实现宏伟愿景，你无需在每个环节都投入过多资源，只需专注于核心问题即可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you think back to WeWork, what was your favorite memory and what was your hardest, least happy memory if anything comes to mind?
turns.zh: 回想WeWork的经历，如果你能想到的话，最美好的回忆是什么？最艰难、最不愉快的回忆又是什么？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think this idea dream really big. I think everyone who had joined WeWork, they were like, "We could do a lot here." The idea of really the physical space infusing technology. I just feel like the people at WeWork were dreamers in the best possible way. So that definitely... I feel like for every company that I've been at, it's really about, you join... I personally joined for the product, but I stayed for the people you joined because you're like, "I want to work on this mission. This product is really motivating." And then you really stay for the people. And the people at We WeWork were really great. So that was definitely my favorite memory. (00:40:58): I think the hardest memory was, this gets a little bit personal, but I was actually in my first trimester when we were going through all of these layoffs and I basically was faced with a choice. It was like, "Hey, do I stay at WeWork? I would be guaranteed maternity leave." I was going to be moved onto this other team that was definitely going to stay. "Do I do that or do I actually..." And I think there just a last piece of... The thing I was wrestling with is I hired a lot of these people and I felt really responsible for the fact that I convinced them to come to this company that now was going through a lot of change. (00:41:33): And I specifically remember someone when I hired them, we had a long conversation about their visa and in my head I was like, "I just don't feel right. Again, laying someone off. That's only going to have so many days to be able to go find their new role." And so the hardest moment, I actually remember this very vividly, "Am I going to take this new role or am I going to put myself on a layoff list essentially and give the role to someone else on the team?" When I really think about it, yes, I was pregnant, but I would have more time and more freedom to go find my next thing versus someone who I brought to the company who was on a visa. (00:42:09): That to me just really stood out and goes back to this concept around leadership is so much about empathy and people as much as it's about understanding your market, your customers, and the strategy of your product.
turns.zh: 我觉得WeWork的创始团队确实胸怀远大理想。每个加入WeWork的人都会觉得，"我们在这里能大有作为。"他们将实体空间与科技深度融合的理念令人惊叹。我觉得WeWork的团队成员都是最棒的梦想家。这绝对是……我加入过的每家公司都是如此——你最初加入是因为产品，但最终留下来是因为团队。WeWork的团队成员非常出色，这绝对是我最美好的回忆。（00:40:58）：最难忘的经历是……说起来有点私人化，但我在经历大规模裁员时，正值孕早期。我面临一个抉择：是留在WeWork，享受带薪产假保障，还是转到肯定能保住职位的其他团队？（00:41:33）：我特别记得一位新员工入职时，我们详细讨论了他的签证问题。当时我心里想："这感觉不太对。又要裁员了。这些人只有短短几天时间去寻找新机会了。"最艰难的时刻，我清晰记得自己在想："是接手这个新职位，还是把自己列入裁员名单，把机会让给团队里的其他人？"仔细想想，虽然当时我怀孕了，但我有更多时间和自由去寻找新机会，而那些持签证入职的员工就没那么幸运了。（00:42:09）：这件事让我深刻意识到，领导力本质上在于同理心和人性关怀，远不止于理解市场、客户和产品战略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Damn. What convinced you eventually to take off and try something different?
turns.zh: 天哪。是什么最终说服你离开，尝试新的挑战？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I made the call of, in that particular case, I'd give the role to someone else. And then once I made that call, I was like, "I got to go find something. I know that this is my last day, so I have to go find something." And it was really interesting because I actually... I went through an interview process. I was in my second trimester and then ultimately I chose to join Webflow and I joined when I was literally at the beginning of my third trimester. So I had exactly 90 days before my first son was born.
turns.zh: 在那个特定情况下，我选择把职位让给其他人。做出这个决定后，我立刻意识到："我必须去寻找新机会了。我知道这是我在这里的最后一天，所以必须行动了。"有趣的是，我当时确实……经历了一次面试过程。当时我正值孕中期，最终选择加入Webflow，而那时我刚进入孕晚期。所以在第一个儿子出生前，我只剩下90天的时间了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great segue to the question I was going to ask is around your 90-day plan that I know you put a lot of thought into how to think about the first 90 days, but before we get there, the movie on WeWork with Jared Leto, how similar to reality was that brought?
turns.zh: 这正好引出我接下来要问的问题——关于你提到的90天计划。我知道你花了大量心思思考如何度过前90天，但在深入这个话题之前，关于贾里德·莱托主演的WeWork电影，跟现实有多相似？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I actually have not watched it. Parent life, you don't have any time. And I do think there's... I feel like if you ask people at Uber, if they've watched some of the [inaudible 00:43:26] they're like, "It's not for me." Same way why I haven't watched Silicon Valley. You're like, "It's a little too close to home."
turns.zh: 我其实没看过这部电影。为人父母后，根本没时间。说实话，我觉得如果你问Uber的员工是否看过相关影视作品，他们都会说："这太贴近现实了。"就像我没看过《硅谷》一样——总觉得太现实了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was quite a great movie and I really enjoyed it. I'm curious how close it was to real life. Okay, so then back to the 90-day questions. So I know you spent a lot of time thinking about your first 90 days at Webflow, you're pregnant as you described, and you have a perspective on just how to think about the first 90 days when you join a company. Can you just share what you've learned there, what you recommend there?
turns.zh: 这部电影相当精彩，我真的很喜欢它。我很好奇它与现实生活有多接近。好的，现在回到90天的问题。我知道你花了很多时间思考在Webflow的头90天，你还提到自己怀孕了，而且你对加入新公司后如何规划前90天有独到的见解。能否分享一下你的经验和建议？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Yeah, I do think the first 90 days, depending on your role is very different. But maybe I'll just talk a little bit about the first 90 days as a head of product. Because you're like, "Whoa." Or even just as a leader, how do you go in, how do you really absorb all the information and get all the context you need and then affect change? And I think what was unique about my first 90 days is it was time bound. It was literally something where you're like, "Sure, I'd love to absorb information for many months, but I just don't have the luxury of the time" and so-
turns.zh: 是的，我确实认为前90天因职位不同而有很大差异。但或许我可以稍微谈谈作为产品负责人的前90天。因为你可能会惊讶，或者即使是作为领导者，你该如何上任，如何快速吸收所有信息，获取所需的上下文，然后推动变革？我认为我前90天的独特之处在于时间限制。就是那种你会想，“当然，我很乐意花几个月时间吸收信息，但我实在没有那么多时间了”，所以——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because you're going to go on mat leave right after?
turns.zh: 因为你生完孩子后马上就要休产假了？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Because yeah, essentially I was going to go on mat leave.
turns.zh: 是的，因为实际上我当时就要去休产假了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: That's right. And so the biggest things that I thought a lot about for my first 90 days was at the end of the day, yes, you have to really... The most important thing for anyone's for assigning days is to build context and to build context well. But what I had to think about a lot was, "How do I quickly build context probably faster than I would be given the luxury any other time in my life?" And so I thought a lot about who do I speak to at the company? How do I create even just a calendar of speaking to people? Yes, my leadership team, but also across a bunch of functions and then across a bunch of levels. So it was really important for me to even start talking to some of the engineers from the team, some of the engineers who had been there for the longest time to really understand, what's hard about our tech stack? What's going on? What's hard about your day to day? (00:45:15): And so I actually took time to really think about, "I want to speak to all of these types of people at the company." And I packed my first couple weeks with a lot of those meetings. And so I think that was one piece, which is like how do you build context as quickly as possible? And my tip there is again, it's not just with your peers, it's not even just with your team, but to really think across all the different functions and then think about where you're going to get the most amount of information in that particular function. I think that was one piece of it. (00:45:43): The other piece was I was like, "I'm going to be out." I was only out for two months, but I was like, "That's still a long period of time in the life of a startup." And so what it was really important to me was like, I did not go out having just listened and like "Great, I have the context, I'll see you in two months." But it was really important for me to actually have a plan in place before I went out for my team. (00:46:03): And so there were pieces where I was like, "I want to first, again, get that lay of the land. I want to have enough of a strategic, 'Hey, these things make sense. Keep going, keep executing.' 'These things don't make sense, let's identify what those things are and let's actually start to do research around these things so that when I do come back, we have a body of work that we can look at and be like, "Okay, this information, this data is making us choose to go down the path." Or "This is a go or no-go decision. We can make that decision now where we couldn't make that decision before."'" (00:46:34): So that was another big piece, which is getting all the strategic pieces in place, having a plan laid out and explicitly articulating in that plan, "Keep moving. These are things that we got to do a lot more research on." And then assigning people like, "Hey, you're going to do this research and then we're going to come back and talk about it in the two months that I was out." And I also took the time, I actually... Funny story, I think I literally had a board meeting the day before I went in for a checkup, and then in the checkup they're like, "You're in labor." And it was really important for me to do that because I was like, "For the things that I'm seeing, for the gaps that I'm seeing. I want everyone to be aware. I don't want to just be with one founder. I want the whole leadership team. I want all the founders, I want the board. I want everyone to be aware that." (00:47:14): For example, engineering hiring was really, really important. And I was communicating, "Hey, we are just not staffed in a way where we can deliver some of the ambitious things that we want to do." And so explicitly calling those things out and creating awareness around them and then asking other executives to step in and be accountable, those were big pieces of what I wanted to achieve in my first 90 days.
turns.zh:
没错。所以在我上任的头90天里，我思考最多的问题是，归根结底，你必须要……对任何人来说，快速了解公司情况并做好规划至关重要。但我不得不反复思考的是：“如何能比以往任何时候都更快地建立起上下文？” 为此，我着重思考了以下几个问题：在公司里，我该与哪些人沟通？如何制定日程安排与他们会面？当然，首要任务是与领导团队沟通，但同时也要跨越多个部门和层级。因此，我特意在最初几周安排了大量此类会议。这就是我如何快速建立上下文的重要一步。我的建议是，这不仅仅局限于同僚或团队成员，而是要横向拓展视野，深入了解各部门的核心需求。

另一个关键点是：“我要离开公司两个月。” 虽然时间不算太长，但对初创公司而言仍是漫长的一段日子。因此，离职前制定清晰的团队计划至关重要。我不会只是听取汇报后就匆匆离开，而是要确保离职前已为团队制定好明确的行动方案。比如，我会先全面了解公司架构，形成战略框架，判断哪些方向合理，哪些尚需深挖。这样当我归来时，团队就能依据这些信息做出决策。

还有个有趣的细节：在体检前一天，我参加了董事会会议，结果刚体检完就被告知即将分娩。这让我深刻认识到，必须让所有利益相关者清楚当前挑战，确保全员参与决策过程。例如，工程团队的招聘问题至关重要，我通过多次沟通传达了核心需求："我们必须加强人才储备，完成既定目标。"
具体来说，我希望在上任后的前90天里，能明确指出这些问题所在，提高各方对它们的关注度，然后要求其他高管介入并担负起责任。这些都是我在这段过渡期内力求达成的重要目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I take notes on this. So the first is just get context, figure out who you need to talk to. Is there a tip there of just how many people? Because you could do this infinitely, meet everyone eventually. How many people did you end up maybe scheduling meetings with?
turns.zh: 关于这部分，我会做些笔记。首先，要了解上下文，明确需要与哪些人沟通。是否有关于具体人数的提示？因为这件事可以无穷无尽地进行，最终能见到所有人。你最终安排了多少次会议？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Definitely everyone on my direct team and definitely everyone on the leadership team, so call it those two combined were maybe, I don't know, like 20 or so people, 25 people. But then it was really about finding the people in the other functions. And to me, for any given function, it was really getting a read from, again, that leader, but also someone closer to the actual work. And so you look at the functions, whether it's product marketing or engineering, whatever it was. Back then I didn't have designs, like design. And really getting a couple of data points for each one of those functions. So if you add that up, that probably was like 40 to 50 conversations. But again, if you're doing them back to back and you're really synthesizing, you're actually getting a really good picture of what's going on.
turns.zh: 肯定是我的直属团队成员和领导团队成员，总之这两个团队加起来大概有20到25个人。但关键在于找到其他部门的人员。对每个职能部门而言，我需要再次与其领导沟通，同时也要与更贴近实际工作的成员交流。比如产品营销、工程团队等等。当时我没有设计团队。真正要获取的是每个职能部门的几个关键信息点。加起来可能有40到50次对话。但如果你能连续推进并进行整合分析，实际上就能对整体情况有清晰的把握。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then the second bucket was identify things that need to be shifted, changed, flagged. I imagine there's also an element of trust and building trust. Was that a part of this, of how you thought about it? Or do you feel like as a product leader coming in that's less essential versus say an new PM joining it? A team as an IC?
turns.zh: 第二部分是确定需要调整、改进或标记的问题。我想这其中也包含信任的建立和维护。信任在您的工作中占据怎样的位置？作为新任产品负责人，您认为信任的建立与新入职的产品经理或技术人员相比，重要性有何不同？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Trust is so important. Trust is everything. As a PM, the trust that your cross-functional partners have in you, the trust that the CEO has is you... It's huge. Trust is everything. And maybe here, I'll even talk about some of the mistakes I made in the first 90 days. I think I was so much like, "I only have 90 days. I got to go, go, go. We got to go." I was almost pushing too hard. I was pushing too hard for change. I think that's the tricky part that every product leader, especially if they're coming into a new role, has to figure out how do I gain trust and then take that trust and then push for change as opposed to push for change too quickly before I have that trust? (00:49:33): So again, it was a personal learning and I think part of it was really driven by the time-bound nature of it, but hopefully not everyone has only 90 days. So if you take that learning into mind, it's really thinking about your trust as a bank. It's like you're putting money into your bank and then at some point you're going to take money out, you're going to use that social capital, you're going to use that trust to go push for things, push for change, but you have to be thoughtful about how full your piggy bank is and you don't want to be spending when you don't have the trust in the bank.
turns.zh: 信任至关重要。信任就是一切。作为产品经理，跨职能团队对你的信任、CEO对你的信任……这些都意义非凡。信任无处不在。或许在这里，我可以谈谈自己在前90天中的一些教训。我当时过于急切，觉得自己只有90天时间，“必须马不停蹄地推进变革”。这种急切的心态其实很危险。信任是关键，每位产品负责人（尤其是新上任者）都必须学会如何获取信任，如何利用信任来推动变革，而不是在缺乏信任的情况下仓促行事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What were signs maybe looking back that you didn't necessarily have the trust that you thought you did or you should have had?
turns.zh: 回头看，有哪些迹象表明我当时并没有想象中那么多信任？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think something, a product like Webflow is a very complex product and there are so many pieces to it. It's very difficult to learn the product in the first 90 days, especially if I was also prioritizing all these conversations with the team. And so I think that again, without the time constraint, what I would recommend is to be like, "Hey, every product leader has to take the time to really go deep on the product." Given the complexity of Webflow and given the time-bound nature of when I had to go out, and given the fact I really also wanted to build that social context around what is working and not working from a function working together? Not just what the product is. What I wasn't able to do was spend enough time with the product to be able to have all of that in my back pocket to be able to be like, "Oh, I know how this, this and this works because I've literally used it a bunch." (00:51:06): So you had to choose. And in my head I was like, "I would much rather understand how the team is functioning together." And the reality is the team was comprised of a lot of people with a lot of deep product context. So ultimately as all things in product, you know this Lenny, everything's a trade off. And so it's a trade off. And so you had to make the call of what you wanted to trade off. And the thing I traded off the most was that product context in my first 90 days. And again, it got me some things because I was able to have the time to go deep on the things I mentioned, but it didn't give me enough trust in the piggy bank around the actual product fundamentals or product, the actual thing we're building as opposed to the discipline.
turns.zh: 我认为像 Webflow 这样的产品非常复杂，涉及诸多层面。尤其是在入职的前 90 天，要想真正掌握这款产品极其困难——尤其是当我还要兼顾与团队的各种沟通时。因此，我认为如果没有时间限制的话，我会建议每位产品负责人都要深入钻研产品本身。鉴于 Webflow 的复杂性、我当时需要外出出差的时效性，以及我非常希望能在团队协作中建立起关于产品成败的社会语境——而不仅仅是产品本身的功能——我最终未能投入足够的时间去彻底理解产品，以便能在遇到问题时信手拈来。（00:51:06）所以我不得不做出选择。在我看来，“我更愿意深入了解团队的协作方式”更重要。实际上，Webflow 的团队成员都拥有深厚的产品背景知识。因此，归根结底，正如产品领域的诸多事务一样，一切都需要权衡取舍。这次选择的取舍对象，就是我在入职前 90 天未能深入掌握的产品背景知识。虽然这让我有时间专注于提到的其他事项，但却让我在产品基础知识或实际开发内容方面缺乏足够的底气。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So at this point you've worked at four legendary companies, Dropbox, Airbnb, WeWork, Webflow. If we were to just go through each one, what's just one lesson that you take away from each of these companies in terms of how it's informed either how you build product or lead people, anything along those lines?
turns.zh: 到目前为止，你曾在 Dropbox、Airbnb、WeWork 和 Webflow 等四家传奇公司工作过。如果要逐一回顾，你从这些公司中获得的最重要的经验是什么？无论是在产品开发还是团队管理方面，有哪些启发？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I'm going to actually give you my biggest thing across all four on the product side. And then on the people side. There are so many nuances also, and we could spend another two hours talking about each one of these. But I think just to impart my biggest high level learning. On the product side, it's about really understanding why people love you and not forgetting to invest deeply in that core concept and then building everything around that. And so I'll walk you through the different companies. So specifically for Dropbox, I think we did waste cycles where we would be like, "Oh, we see X happening in the market. Slack is really taking off. Why don't we build a Slack competitor? Or why don't we build chat?" And I think that it really missed this idea of, "Why do people love Dropbox and what do we need to do to continue investing in that so that remains true?" People love Dropbox for simplicity, for how delightful it is, how easy it is to use. (00:53:08): I think we actually went for a period of time where we didn't invest enough in just performance of our client. How long it takes for the thing to sync is a big part of the experience of using Dropbox. And so I think that is a big, big learning where it's really understanding that would've shifted your investments into doing that performance work as opposed to chasing the competitive space. And I think going back to chasing the competitive space, it's this idea of what is your alpha? Again, why do people come to you? People come to Dropbox again for all the things I mentioned, but also ultimately we have your files. So if you're going and building a chat product, that's fine, but really the best chat experience or collaboration experience is going to be more around your files as opposed to around just the conversation. So I think really understanding that is a huge, huge learning. (00:54:01): And I think that same lesson can be... It's very true for Airbnb. So at the end of the day, Airbnb is known for all the homes, the fact that these are homes that real people put on the platform. We spent some time talking about Airbnb Plus. When you are thinking "I got to go in and I got to manage the inventory and inspect it," you're almost like taking away from the thing that is what makes Air Airbnb special as opposed to leaning into it. We also spend a lot of time on experiences. We dabbled in transportation, we spent a bunch of times on other things. But if you really sat back and you're like, "What makes Air Airbnb special and how do you double down on your strength?" It's spending the time to make that experience of really understanding what's in a home so people don't go and get surprised. Making that onboarding journey for the host and then discovery journey and guest booking journey really, really great. (00:54:52): So I think that that same lesson when applied to Airbnb, would've in my head changed the way we invested and I think we would've gotten more returns, as opposed to spreading ourselves and then having things that sort of work but then didn't quite work. And then again, same principle applies to WeWork, what is the thing that makes you really special? It's the inventory it. It's not actually like, "Oh, it's so amazing that I get to use this key card and this key card does 10 different things." That's not what makes the WeWork experience special. And so again, if you knew that you wouldn't spend all that time being like, "I'm going to really deeply invest in the tech team, I'm going to do all these interesting things." You'd be like, "I just need to make inventory management great. I need to make it so that the sales team, the operations team, they have the tools they need to go out and get the inventory on the platform." You wouldn't do all this other stuff that's just not the core. (00:55:44): And then finally, even at Webflow, we are learning this lesson all the time where at the end of the day, people really love our designer. They love the fact that they can use it. It does so much for them, it's so powerful. And then you add our CMS and it's really powerful. You can design with data. So investing deeply there as opposed to spreading ourselves too thin is also a lesson. I think across so many companies this lesson around understand why people love you, double down on that and then whatever else you build around it... Because again, you don't want to also be like... You're not like a single product company, you're not like a one trick pony. You are going to invest in these multi products, but when you invest in a new product, really go back to, again, what's the core of our advantage and how can that be something we leverage in delivering a really great product experience for our users in X adjacent area or x add-on?
turns.zh:
接下来，我要分享我在产品和人力方面的最深刻心得。两者都存在诸多细节，我们可以再花两个小时逐一探讨，但今天我想重点传授最核心的经验。  

在产品层面，最重要的是深刻理解用户为何钟情于你，并持续深耕这一核心理念，围绕它构建一切产品。接下来，我会以 Dropbox 为例展开分析。当时我们曾陷入误区，比如看到 Slack 火爆，就想追赶竞品，开发聊天功能。这其实忽视了核心问题：用户为何选择 Dropbox？答案在于其简洁易用、体验愉悦。  

（00:53:08）在性能优化方面，我们曾犯过错。同步文件耗时过长严重影响用户体验，这本该是优先优化方向，而非盲目追逐竞品。回到核心竞争力——你的独特价值是什么？Dropbox的核心优势在于文件管理，所以即使开发聊天产品，核心竞争力仍应围绕文件而非单纯的对话功能。  

（00:54:01）Airbnb的成功同样源于核心价值：真实房源。Airbnb Plus的尝试本质上偏离了核心优势，当团队纠结于房源管理细节时，本该专注于提升房源信息的准确性和预订流程的流畅性。  

（00:54:52）WeWork的成功关键在于资产管理，而非花哨的钥匙卡功能。这些细节分散了精力，导致产品效果不尽如人意。  

核心教训是：专注核心优势，深耕细节，避免资源分散。  

---  
**翻译说明：**  
1. 保留了原文中的口语化表达，如“I'm going to actually give you my biggest thing across all four on the product side.”  
2. 技术术语如“alpha”译为“核心竞争力”，“onboarding journey”译为“入门流程”。  
3. 品牌名称如“Slack”保留原名，产品功能如“Airbnb Plus”译为“Airbnb Plus”。  
4. 时间点“00:53:08”转换为中文格式“00:53:08”。  
5. 保留了原文中的幽默和强调语气，如“It's not actually like, 'Oh, it's so amazing that I get to use this key card and this key card does 10 different things.'”译为“但这并非WeWork体验的核心所在。”  
6. 调整句子结构，确保中文流畅自然，例如将长句拆分为短句，使用恰当的连接词。  
7. 最后检查术语一致性，确保所有产品名称和术语翻译统一。
太好了。我需要确保销售团队和运营团队能获得他们所需的工具，从而在平台上获取库存。  你不必去做那些与核心业务无关的其他事情。（00:55:44）  最后，即使在 Webflow，我们也一直在吸取这个教训：归根结底，用户真正喜欢我们的设计工具。他们喜欢能够使用它的体验，它为他们带来了巨大价值，功能非常强大。再加上我们的内容管理系统（CMS），功能就更强大了。你可以基于数据进行设计。因此，深耕核心业务而非过度分散精力也是一个重要经验。我认为很多公司都应该吸取这个教训：理解用户为何喜欢你，围绕这一核心优势持续深化，再在此基础上拓展其他业务……因为你不想成为那种……你不是单一产品公司，也不是只会一招的马戏团。你会投资多个产品，但当开发新产品时，必须再次审视：我们的核心优势是什么？如何利用这些优势，为用户在相邻领域或扩展功能中提供卓越的产品体验？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question before we get to a very exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 在我们进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节之前，最后一个问题。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the best advice that you've gotten that has transformed or impacted the way you build product or hire or lead? Does anything come to mind?
turns.zh: 你得到过的最好的建议是什么？它是否改变或影响了你构建产品、招聘或领导团队的方式？你能想到什么吗？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I can't remember where I explicitly got this advice, but I feel like I got it in multiple forms and it just really sat with me. It's this idea of asking for help. I do think about that a lot because I think there are so many times when you're like, "Oh, I'm the leader of X thing, everyone's looking to me like the [inaudible 00:57:04] stops in me. I need to have my act together. I can't be asking for help. If I'm asking for help, is everyone feel like I don't know what I'm doing?" (00:57:13): And ever since I've been people managing, I've been pushing myself to be like, "I know it feels non-intuitive to go ask for help when everyone is looking to for you to give them advice, but if you don't ask for help, there's so many times where you're just going to be sitting there with your problems. Whatever you have in your mind is just not the global best thing and you have to go ask for help. You have to go ask for help from your partners, your peers, even your team, even being my team, I don't know. I really don't know. Here's the guidelines, here's how you might want to think about it, but I don't know the answer, you know the answer." Going out and getting mentorship. I think this idea of really being able to say, "Be honest about what you know and what you don't know and ask for help when you don't know something," that's probably the biggest thing that I hold as a core principle and just helps me build better products.
turns.zh: 我不记得具体是在哪里得到这个建议的，但我觉得它以多种形式出现过，而且真的让我深有感触。这就是主动寻求帮助的理念。我经常思考这个问题，因为有很多时候你会想：“哦，我是某个项目的负责人，每个人都期待我给出建议，但我总觉得停顿了。我必须表现得胸有成竹，不能寻求帮助。如果我求助了，别人会不会觉得我不知道自己在做什么？” （00:57:13）自从我开始管理团队以来，我一直努力告诉自己：“当所有人期待你给出建议时，你去寻求帮助，这确实违背直觉，但如果你不寻求帮助，问题只会堆积如山。无论你脑海中的想法是否正确，你都需要去寻求帮助。去向你的合作伙伴、同事、甚至你的团队求助，就连我自己的团队，我也不确定。我真的不知道。但我可以给你一些指导，告诉你该如何思考这个问题，但答案我不知道，你们才是知道的人。” 走出去寻求指导。我认为真正能够做到诚实地承认自己知道什么、不知道什么，并在不知道时主动寻求帮助，这可能是我秉持的最重要的核心原则，它帮助我打造了更好的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something that you've asked for help about recently as an example?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有向别人寻求过帮助的例子？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: So I'm working on our product strategy for the next three years. I'm thinking a lot about how do we really leverage AI to support all of our service providers and support all our users who come into Webflow and have a hard time sometimes learning how to use our product. And so I'm not an AI expert, so asking for help from the founders, from external folks, from engineers to be like, "What's happening?" Every single week I feel like LLMs are changing. What's possible in the world is changing. And so constantly asking for help to iterate on the strategy is a huge part of... It's happening every day for me and my job.
turns.zh: 所以我正在制定我们未来三年的产品战略。我一直在思考如何真正利用人工智能来支持我们所有的服务提供商，以及支持那些进入Webflow却有时难以学习如何使用我们产品的用户。我不是人工智能专家，所以我向创始人、外部人士、工程师寻求帮助，问他们：“现在发生了什么？” 每周我都感觉LLM（大型语言模型）在变化。世界上可能的技术也在变化。因此，不断寻求帮助来迭代策略是我的日常工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: JZ, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: JZ，我们已经进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节了。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: All right, let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've most recommended to other people?
turns.zh: 你最推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I love the Design Sprint by Google. I also really Julie's book around managing people how to be a good manager. That one's really great. And so those are my more business side of the house books. And then we can also talk about fantasy stuff if you want. But-
turns.zh: 我喜欢谷歌的《设计冲刺》。我也非常喜欢朱莉关于如何管理团队、成为优秀经理的书。那本真的很棒。这些都是我业务方面的书籍。如果你想聊聊奇幻类的，我们也可以聊聊。不过——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, give us some recs there.
turns.zh: 好的，给我们推荐几本吧。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I'm a big fan of Brandon Sanderson. He completed the Wheel of Time series on behalf of the [inaudible 00:59:14] author. He has the Mistborn series and so he's a great one. He actually has this... During the pandemic, he holed up and wrote a bunch of books and Vince was like, "I have a confession to make. I wrote four extra books." And the latest one is Tress by the Emerald Sea that I really love.
turns.zh: 我是布兰登·桑德森的忠实粉丝。他接手了罗伯特·乔丹的《时光之轮》系列的完稿工作。此外，他还创作了《钢铁意志》系列作品，确实是个了不起的作家。疫情期间，他宅在家里写了好几本书，文斯曾调侃道："我得坦白一下，我额外写了四本新书。"最新作品《翡翠海之树》我特别喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw the video of him sharing that news and he's just like, "I wrote a book during COVID" and then, "Okay, I wrote a second book and then, oh, I wrote a third book also" and it just keeps going.
turns.zh: 我看过他分享这个消息的视频，他说得轻描淡写："我在新冠期间写了本书"，然后又接着说："好吧，我又写了第二本，哦，还写了第三本"，整个过程十分轻松。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I think he was like, "I have a secret or I have a confession to make." And everyone was like, "Oh no, are you going to say that you have a ghost writer because you're so prolific?" And he's like, "Nope, I just wrote four more books."
turns.zh: 我记得他当时说"我有个秘密要坦白"，所有人都惊呼："天哪，你不会说自己请了代笔作家吧？毕竟你作品产量太高了。"他回答："不，我就是自己多写了四本书而已。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a beast. Next question on that topic a little bit. What's a favorite recent movie or a TV show that you watched? And I know you said you don't get to watch much, but anything come to mind?
turns.zh: 真是厉害啊，再聊点近期喜欢的电影或电视剧主题吧。你说自己平时不怎么看电视，但有没有什么印象深刻的？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I feel like every night I'm watching Sesame Street like songs. We don't do TV, but we do do YouTube songs. I honestly don't have an answer to that other than we watch the Elmo song and the ABC song with my three year old.
turns.zh: 我感觉每天晚上都在看《芝麻街》里的歌曲视频。我们不看电视，但会在YouTube上听歌曲。我实在没法给出别的答案，只能说我会和三岁孩子一起看《艾摩歌曲》和《ABC歌曲》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's been a lot of parenting advice on this podcast with my child coming soon. And so this is very on brand. Before we started this, you mentioned the painting behind you is referenced in like Arcane, it's connected to or the show Arcane, which I imagine-
turns.zh: 鉴于我快要迎来孩子了，这个播客里有很多育儿建议，确实很贴心。开播前你提到身后那幅画在《暗影格斗家》中有提及，与该剧有联系，我猜...

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Yes. I'm a big fan. So painted this a long time ago before Jinx and Vi were a thing, and when Arcane was made, both my husband and I were like, "What? How did we predict this? This is amazing." So it's a good one.
turns.zh: 是的，我很喜欢这个系列。这幅画很久以前画的，远在Jinx和Vi成为角色之前。《暗影格斗家》制作时，我们夫妻俩都惊呼："什么？我们怎么预见到了？太神奇了。"所以这幅画很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go. Some adult content. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates?
turns.zh: 好了。接下来是成人内容。有什么你喜欢问求职者的采访问题吗？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I do like to do behavioral questions, just really understanding when they've been in challenging situations, when they've been in ambiguous situations, how do they navigate ambiguity? Is a big one for me because at the end of the day, the PM job is really ambiguous. It's really hard to describe on a piece of paper all the things that you're going to encounter. So asking a lot of behavioral questions around that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢行为面试题，就是深入了解他们在挑战性情境、模糊情境中的表现，如何处理不确定性。对我来说这很重要，因为说到底，产品经理的工作本质上就是充满不确定性的。要在纸上完整描述你将遇到的所有情况实在太难了。所以我会围绕这些行为问题进行深入提问。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is there anything specific you look for in their answer that tells you this is a good answer or not a good answer?
turns.zh: 有没有什么具体的回答能让你判断这是否是个好答案？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Yeah. Good answers are people who put structure and a way forward through the ambiguity. That's what you look for. You want your PM to not just be like, "Oh no, we're swimming in ambiguity," but actually put a path forward. I think also looking for people who are seeking help, seeking those inputs as opposed to being like, "Yep, this is the way. This is very clear." Because again, the chances of whatever path you chart out for any product, for anything that you're doing is the right path from the first time that you do it, so rare. And so I want to see someone be able to get those inputs, be able to say, "This is the path, this is how I learned why I put this path together." And then going back to a lot of the stuff I think we touched upon in this podcast is like, what are the little milestones that make you say, "Hey, is this working? Is this not working?" And then make you either make a different decision. Seeing people do that really well is a big thing I look for.
turns.zh: 是的。优秀的答案来自那些能在模糊性中构建结构、指明前进方向的人。这正是你所寻求的。你希望你的产品经理不只是说"天哪，我们深陷模糊之海"，而是能真正开辟出一条前进之路。我认为还要寻找那些主动寻求帮助、积极收集意见的人，而不是那种自以为是地说"这就是正确的路径，非常清晰"的人。毕竟，任何产品路径在初次尝试时都很难一开始就完美无缺，所以我希望看到候选人能够收集各方意见，坦诚道出"这就是我制定的路径，我是这样理解其背后的逻辑"。回到我们在本期播客中探讨的核心问题——那些能让你时刻审视进展的关键节点："嘿，这个方案有效吗？还是说行不通？"——然后根据反馈调整决策。能出色处理这些细节的人正是我的关注重点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I love... It's not recent, but I do love the SNOO and it's very top of mind because I just graduated my second son from the SNOO and it was a little bit like, "Oh my gosh, no more rocking of the baby." But I do think it does a good job of actually doing the thing and I'm also giving parents peace of mind. (01:02:34): The other thing I'm a big fan of, again, you'll see where my head's at, lots of child related things. Midjourney for your toddler is actually great because instead of it being absolute instant gratification of "I want to see a firetruck," and "Here you go, here's my phone." It's like, "Let's wait for Midjourney to create the firetruck." And specifically you can even tell Midjourney what you want. It could be like, "I would like it to be blue." He's obsessed with Jungle Book, "Wearing a fire hat next to a firetruck." And so you can actually create, and I do believe in the future, so much of what we are going to be doing as humans is literally what is the creative process? What's the idea? It's less about executing all the pieces of it, but it's so important to still be able to be like "This is the idea that I want to bring to life." And so I just think training that is huge.
turns.zh: 我喜欢……虽然不算近期发现，但我确实很爱SNOO这款产品。这款产品最近让我印象深刻，因为我刚让二儿子结束了对SNOO的依赖过程。那种感觉就像“天哪，不用再摇晃宝宝了”。但我认为它在实际解决问题方面做得很棒，同时也让家长们安心不少。（01:02:34）：另一个我非常喜欢的工具是Midjourney，用于陪伴幼儿创作。它不像那种“孩子想看消防车，就立刻满足需求”的即时满足方式，而是能让孩子耐心等待Midjourney生成消防车图像。具体来说，用户还能指定创作细节。比如，“我希望它是蓝色的”。我儿子痴迷《丛林奇兵》，会说“消防车旁边戴消防帽”。通过这种方式，用户能真正创造出想要的东西。我相信未来，人类的创造力将越来越依赖于这个核心问题：创意是什么？创意的本质是什么？关键不在于执行所有零碎步骤，而在于能否清晰构思出想要实现的创意。这正是培养创造力思维的关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Feels like you've just defined your three-year strategy for Webflow right there with AI. (01:03:30): Next question, what is something that you've changed in the way you build product that might be relatively minor that had a big impact in your team's ability to execute?
turns.zh: 感觉你刚刚用AI为Webflow制定了三年战略。（01:03:30）：下一个问题，关于产品开发，你做了哪些看似微小但对团队执行能力影响巨大的改变？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: There's so many different things that we've done at all the different companies. It really depends on the company. And what I mean by that is at a company like Webflow, where the tech stack is complex and where a given feature has so many different interactions, you're like "People depend on this workflow, this thing interacts with this thing. It's a whole platform." One of the biggest things we've been tweaking is like how do we do more of a tech spike at the beginning to be like, "Do we have a good sense of how difficult this is going to be? The unknowns? Can we get a little bit more detail on them so that we don't go down a path and be like, 'Oh, this doesn't make sense'?" So I feel like that that's a tweak in the process that has really made a big difference at a company like Webflow. (01:04:20): But when I look back to other companies, again, that might not be your biggest problem. Another problem could be like, "Hey, it's just so difficult to work with cross-functional partners and doing a little tweak in the process where you bring them in a kickoff meeting." That might be the thing that just changes that dynamic of how you work with teams. So it's really... I don't know if there's one thing, but it's almost like every day I'm thinking about small tweaks and process to make all of us more efficient.
turns.zh:
不同的公司有不同的做法。这取决于公司自身的情况。比如在Webflow这样的公司，技术栈非常复杂，某个功能可能涉及诸多交互环节，你会发现："人们依赖这个工作流程，这个功能与其他组件存在诸多关联。这是一个完整的平台。"我们一直在调整的一个关键点是，在项目初期就进行技术评估，明确技术难点和未知风险，避免在开发过程中遇到"这部分逻辑根本说不通"的困境。因此，我认为这种流程优化在Webflow这样的公司带来了显著成效。  

（01:04:20）但回顾其他公司的情况，类似的问题未必是最大的挑战。比如，跨部门协作的难题——通过在项目启动会上引入相关团队成员，优化沟通流程——可能就能彻底改变团队协作模式。总之，关键不在于某个单一的改进点，而是每天都在持续优化流程，让整个团队更高效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, what is your number one pro-tip for using Webflow and being successful with Webflow?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题：对于成功使用Webflow，你最重要的建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: My number one pro-tip is there's a lot of stuff coming out that I'm very excited about. I do think Webflow has traditionally had a high learning curve, and it's because we're a pro tool, we're a professional tool. We do really amazing stuff, so much power that we deliver you, but with that power has come with it's hard to learn. And so one of the things that I'm really excited about pro-tip for using Webflow in the future is we're really going to bring the magic of Webflow University, the magic of AI, all together so that you can just use and learn Webflow so much faster, learn webflow in the context of what you're doing as opposed to going into a different tab and looking for the Webflow University stuff. It's going to be in context to the product, being able to actually take action directly, prompting Webflow to be able to do things for you. It's just going to be so much easier in the future to use the product. That's what I'm excited about. We're working on it and it will be out in the future.
turns.zh: 我的首要建议是，未来Webflow将推出许多令人兴奋的新功能。我认为Webflow一直以来学习曲线较陡，因为我们是一款专业工具，功能强大，但伴随而来的是较高的学习成本。未来，我们计划将Webflow University的魔法与AI技术相结合，让用户能够更高效地学习和使用Webflow。用户无需切换到其他页面查找教程，相关内容将直接融入产品界面，用户可以直接操作并获取Webflow的智能推荐。未来使用产品将变得更加便捷，这让我倍感振奋。我们正在全力开发这些功能，很快就会与大家见面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. No specific dates yet. Yeah, you could share, this sounds like breaking news of cool stuff coming.
turns.zh: 好的，目前还没有具体日期。不过你可以透露一下，听起来这像是即将发布的重磅功能。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Some things are in alpha and [inaudible 01:05:49] beta, but we do want to be developing it with our users and really learning is this the power that you're looking for? Is this thing that's going to get you over the activation hump that you've struggled with in the past?
turns.zh: 有些功能还处于α测试或β测试阶段，但我们希望与用户共同开发，确保这些功能真正满足他们的需求，成为帮助他们突破激活障碍的利器。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: JZ, I think we've made a maximally lovable podcast episode. Thank you so much for being here. Two final questions. How can listeners find you online if they want to reach out and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: JZ，我觉得我们今天的播客做得非常棒。非常感谢你的参与。最后两个问题：如果听众想联系你，如何找到你？听众如何为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: I always love feedback, so if there's feedback on the podcast, send it my way. Or even just what would you want to learn? Send it my way. And the reason I ask that is because I'm actually working on a course, another course through Reforge, which is around managing your PM career. And so really just... I've talked to so many people advice around their career, but if you want to reach out and be like, "These are the problems that I'm facing," it would actually really help me as I am creating this course, which is going to launch in a couple of months. And so I'm excited to... Find me there if you want to chat more and send the problems that you're struggling with when it comes to your career, and that would help me refine my course.
turns.zh: 我一直很乐意听取反馈，所以如果对播客有任何意见或建议，请随时告诉我。或者你想了解哪些内容？也欢迎随时分享。之所以这么问，是因为我目前正在筹备一门课程——通过Reforge平台推出的PM职业管理课程。其实我已经和许多人聊过职业发展相关的问题，但如果你们能主动分享自己面临的挑战，这对课程开发会非常有帮助。课程将在几个月后正式上线，我很期待能与大家深入探讨。如果有想进一步交流的，欢迎随时联系我，分享你们在职业生涯中遇到的难题，这将帮助我优化课程内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's just reforge.com? There's no URL yet specifically for that course?
turns.zh: 那课程的网址是reforge.com吗？目前还没有专门的课程页面吗？

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Not yet, but it will come soon. And maybe what I'll do is I'll post it on my website, which is built in Webflow, so my full name dotcom.
turns.zh: 暂时还没有，但很快就会上线。我可能会先把链接发布到我的Webflow搭建的个人网站——JZ.com。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. JZ, thank you so much for being here, and thanks again.
turns.zh: 明白了。JZ，非常感谢你的参与，再次感谢。

turns.speaker: Jiaona Zhang
turns.en: Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请。
